blocks.x: All right, I'll just put the introduction on then. This is being recorded at 935 7th Street, the home of Joe Lycanum, August 20th, 1959. That's right, isn't it? 20th?

blocks.s: Mrs. Joe Loyacano (wife of Joe Loyacano)
blocks.x: Yes, sir.
I think so, yeah.
Well, let's get your name on here correctly, Mr. Lycanum.
Joseph Lycanum.
Oh, good. And Paul? Paul Crawford. And you're Mrs. Lycanum. I see. That's your full name, Joseph Lycanum?
Yeah, they used to call me Hook. On account of the noise.
Daniel Mello was telling about you and Pansy Lane kidding each other.
Yeah, we got all our hair shaved off one time.
Is that right?
We got a shave with a razor. Got their hair all cut off and then the head shaved with a razor.
Just for fun, or?
That's all, just for the kicks. You could pull a handkerchief over our head with a silk handkerchief without it sticking.

blocks.s: Mrs. Joe Loyacano (wife of Joe Loyacano)
blocks.x: Yeah, but when they were playing that time, it used to be Dixieland. They used to call it Ragtime. Then from Ragtime it went to Dixieland, and then from Dixieland, now it's the Dixieland Jazz. They then put it in three stages, and then they tried to get that stage out with all the progressive. But he played that when he first came to see me. That's near 45 years ago. I mean, it ain't new to him.
Yeah, I've been in the business just 50 years when I give it up.
How long have you not been playing?
Since January.
Since January 1959.
That's right.
When were you born, if you don't mind us asking?
I was born October the 14th in 93.

blocks.s: Mrs. Joe Loyacano (wife of Joe Loyacano)
blocks.x: It'll be 66 this coming October.
This coming October the 14th, I'll be 66 years old.
Good. Did you have any lessons when you started playing trombone?
No, no. I started by playing the pianola. Remember the electric pianos you pump with your foot? Well, I pumped with my feet, and I played with my hands and mouth. And I learned the trombone that way.
Was trombone your first instrument?
That was my very first instrument, yeah.
And did anybody else in your family play music?
Yeah, my brothers played music. I had three brothers play music.
And what were their names?
Arnold, Jack. And Bud.
And what instruments did they play?
Well, Bud played mandolin. He played guitar. He played a little drum. He played a little bass. He played a little violin. Arnold played a little piano, bass, drum. Guitar, mandolin.
Jack, he played just...
Jack played trombone.
Was he left-handed?
Yeah, left-handed trombone player.
I've heard of him.
Yeah.
I can't remember if I was a picture of somebody playing trombone. What kind of a trombone did you start? On a slide or a vowel?
On a slide, yeah. Slide trombone. And I used to pedal the piano with my feet and I'd play the Trimone with my hands and my mouth.
What kind of music and songs did you hear when you first started?
Well, regular old time jazz songs. That time we used to call them ragtime tunes.
Do you remember the names of any of them?
No, God, I don't, man. Fifty years ago was a long time to remember the names of any of them tunes.

blocks.s: Mrs. Joe Loyacano (wife of Joe Loyacano)
blocks.x: Well, I think they had, you know, they used to play, I know plenty of them. I can't just remember myself what they were.
Oh no, that's too far back to remember.

blocks.s: Mrs. Joe Loyacano (wife of Joe Loyacano)
blocks.x: And he played, after that you went with the Majada Brothers, with the Triangle Band. You used to play for Lou Rose.

I played with Jack Lane's Old Reliance Band. That was the first band I ever worked with. Jack Lane's Old Reliance Band. Then I worked with Pansy Lane. Then I left Pansy and I went to work with Dan Hughes. We used to advertise for Lou Rose's Burles show by walking around Canal Street two hours every evening. And that, that, oh that went on for about two years. We used to advertise every night from, from eight, from six to eight. Walking around Canal Street. I had some pictures of that around here, but I don't know where they are. My daughter has them somewhere around here.

blocks.s: Mrs. Joe Loyacano (wife of Joe Loyacano)
blocks.x: I can't give you them, that's why I said it's here.

Oh, well we just want to look. We'll bring the camera by sometime and maybe take some pictures after I learn how to make those copy pictures. Yeah. Uh, I was wondering, uh, Dan Hughes had some favorite tune, didn't he Paul? What was that Raymond was telling us about? Persian Rose? Was he the one who played Persian Rose all the time?

No, not that I know of. Dan, Dan had any, any tune was his favorite tune. He had one eye and he was a trumpet player. He went, he went, he finally wound up with the dogs at the Greyhound, Greyhound races. Dog races.
He went to the dogs?
Yeah, he went to the dogs.
Uh, who was in Jack Lane's band when you started?
Jack Lane's band? My God, I don't remember. I don't remember, to tell you the truth. I couldn't remember one man that was in that band.
I guess you were quite young at the time.
Oh yeah, I was only a kid. I was merely a kid at that time.
Were you in short bands?
Yeah, 16 years old. Oh.
Do you remember who any of the fellas with the Pansy Lane's band were?
I remember that, uh, Leon Mello's brother played drum.
Sam, I guess, huh?
We used to call him Foots. Bigfoot. We used to call him Foots Mello. And Harry Shields played clarinet. Pansy played trumpet. And, uh, who played piano now? I don't remember who played piano with us.
They had pianos back in those days.

Oh yeah, sure we had piano with us. Sure. And I remember when I played with, uh, Joe Ellibush's band. We never had no piano at that time. We used to play lawn parties. And they never had no pianos at the lawn parties. So you used to have to use the guitar or banjo.
Who was Joe Ellibush?
He was a trombone player. Terrible trombone player. But he was, he went around as a trombone player anyhow.
He got the job.
He got the, he was the boss man. Yeah, he got the job so he was the leader.
And what were you playing?
I was playing bass fiddle. Bass horn.
I wanted to ask you about trombone players when you first started. Were any of them on valve at all?
Yeah, Bill Galois.
He was still using the valve.
Still using the valve trombone, yeah.
Well, could they make the slides, you know, the glisses on the valve at all?
No, no, not, not anymore than you could make it on a trumpet. Same, same as making it on a trumpet with the valve sliding up.
Mm-hmm. And what kind of a style would they, would he play on valve trombone? Would it be just a vamp or would it be more complicated than that?

Well, sometimes he played vamp, sometimes he played a little more complicated than vamp style. See, when I played trombone, I played mostly vamp style trombone myself. I played mostly bass parts on a trombone.
Did they have much range on trombone in those days? Much range?
Yes. No, no. The range wasn't high at all. Low range. Played in the low register most of the time.
Where would you work from, say, from low, about, you know, the low note to the high note?
Oh, you'd work, well, from about the seventh position on up to the first position.
Seven down low E or?
Yeah, all the way up to the first position.
You mean all the way on the bottom of the horn?
Yeah, all the way down the end of the slide. Yeah. And then how high would you work? All the way up to the top.
I mean up, say, would you play F, you know, the high F?

No, I don't think I'd hit it that high. Not that high? No, I don't think I'd hit it that high. See, I never read a note of music at that time. I didn't know nothing about music. All I knew was grab my horn and go, this fella would say, well, we're going to play such a tune, let's go. And I'd hit him in the slide and we'd go ahead with it.
Did you take any lessons in the meantime?

No, I never took a lesson in my life. Not a one, huh? Never took a lesson in my life. I went one time to take lessons with a man by the name of Wickfold, who happened to be the trombonist at the Orphan Theater. And he was a very good teacher. So after the first time I went to his house, he told me, he said, son, there's no use of you coming here. He said, I couldn't teach you anything. He said, you're just a fraction of a second behind me all the time. He said, you don't know what the hell you're doing. So he said, I don't want your money because I don't need it. He said, but I never could. If I could learn you how to play trombone, but by music, he said, I'd learn you for nothing. I'd teach you for nothing.
You're just picking up everything by ear, huh?

Yeah, I was playing. He was telling me this, now you do this and do that. And he'd pick up his horn and he'd do it and I was right with him, you see. And he was just the least bit behind him. So that he didn't know half the time whether I was reading and I was just playing along with him.
She's got some pictures here she was showing.
That's some pictures of Batusi's orchestra in Biloxi.

blocks.s: Mrs. Joe Loyacano (wife of Joe Loyacano)
blocks.x: That's what's in Biloxi. I don't know who's this but Sharky I think down in the Oop Parade.
It looks like Sharky but I can't care.
Yeah, this is with Sharky I tell you. That's the Silver Slipper. That's Sharky right there.
Who are the other guys?
You recognize them? That's Sharky on trumpet, Mike Ryan on drums, myself on bass, Johnny Gregory on sax, and Johnny Miller on piano.
That looks like a baritone, huh?
Yeah, I don't know.
Baritone sax, I believe.
No, he played alto and tenor.
Mardi Gras picture, huh?
Yeah, no that was at the Silver Slipping. It's now the Dream Room.
It says, welcome Mardi Gras on it.
Yeah, well that was during the Mardi Gras season. That was taken during the Mardi Gras season.
I wonder what year that was about, do you remember?

No, I don't have any idea what year this was in. That must be over 25 years ago. Oh yeah, that's over 25 years ago. Now those were taken in Biloxi in the Elks Club in Biloxi. You see this is the, this here blacked out part is the death, death of the different Elks that died in the head. Oh yeah. Blacking it out. But you see that's Johnny Bertucci playing trumpet there. That's Harry Tosen playing clarinet. That's Avery La Pazza playing piano. Myself playing trombone and Ellis Stratikas playing drums.

blocks.s: Mrs. Joe Loyacano (wife of Joe Loyacano)
blocks.x: Well did you tell them when you learned how to play really? When you learned how to play the trombone by notes? When you went to Club Forest?
Well I didn't learn to play trombone by notes when I went to Club Forest. When I went to Club Forest I went on sousaphone and bass fiddle.

blocks.s: Mrs. Joe Loyacano (wife of Joe Loyacano)
blocks.x: Well where did you learn to play the notes?

I learned to play by music when I went to work with Max Fink at the Lill Club. Oh. On the barone between St. Joseph and Julia. Max Fink used to pair everything from cover to cover you know. And I was playing sousaphone and I had to get the parts out because he didn't want anybody to know that I was the only faker in the band. So I'd get the parts out for every tune and I noticed that when I started it at this cover and I'd finish up with that cover every time I'd hit one particular note it would be on this particular valve. So eventually it would come to me that I could read music and that's how I started to read. Fantastic. That's how I read. Nobody taught me a thing. Ain't a man in this world can say he ever taught me how to read a note. Like I told you, Wick Bolt said if I could teach you to play music, he said I'd teach you for nothing. But he said your ear is too sharp. He said you're just a fraction of a second behind me. He said you ain't fooling me. You're fooling yourself. He said because you're paying me and I don't need your money. So he'd give me up. He wouldn't fooling me.

That's an article here I noticed. It's a column called Know Your Coast. It's from the Biloxi paper. Monday afternoon, December the 29th, 1958. Yeah. So that picture with Johnny Bertuzzi was taken in January of 1920.
Yeah.
So we'll have to get this article. That'll be good. Uh, did you ever know a fellow named Peck Kelly?
Yeah. I knew Peck Kelly when he was in Texas.
Mm-hmm.
Yeah, I knew Peck. But I never worked with him.
You never worked with him?
No, no. I worked in Texas with Wingy Manone. San Antonio, Texas.
I wondered. I saw something about you being with Peck Kelly.
No, I never was with Peck Kelly. No, not me. No, uh-uh. I never was with Peck.
And that was Wingy's band in San Antonio?
Yeah, that was Wingy's band, yeah.
Do you remember any of the people in it?

Well, they had, uh, Wingy on Trumpet. They had, uh, Pee Wee Russell. 

on clarinet they had a fella by the name of Humphreys playing drums and a kid from Baton Rouge I can't think of his name now he played saxophone little short young fella played saxophone we had a pretty nice band Wingy did you worked other places with Wingy too I guess yeah I worked in for luck he was winging at the Buena Vista hotel in the White House hotel and who did he have there at the Buena Vista we had uh Mike Ryan on drums we had uh Bob Sackerman on saxophone I don't know if you know Sackerman no I don't well he he's he got killed in Chicago got rolled over the car he's he'd been a good age now he was playing saxophone and Wingy played trumpet T Gordon played trombone for a while and uh then Merritt Brunus played trombone for a while and uh not Merritt but Henny Brunus played trombone for a while and uh what did he have on clarinet I don't remember who he had on clarinet but he had a probably had a pretty good lineup of men

Well what kind of tunes did you play in general? Would you play polkas at all?
Play polkas, foxtrots, one steps, waltzes, lances, varieties, all that kind of stuff. Ever play any quadrilles? No, I don't think I remember of ever playing any of them.
Oh, about the Triangle Band, what was that like? Was that a spot job band?

Yeah, that was strictly a spot job band. That was two Majana brothers, Sato and Tony Majana. And I played trombone with them for a while, then Leon Mello went in, took my place when I quit them. I quit them, we had a little run in about, I went after a job and I got the job and the first night on the job they showed up late and I got balled out for it and I tore them off and I quit the band.
Where did Tony Majana play? Trumpet.

Ballet Rite.

Bud, my oldest brother.

segments.title: Opening of the Loyacano interview at his home
segments.summary: Crawford announces the recording at Loyacano's home on August 20, 1959 and confirms names.

segments.title: Nickname Hook and the head-shaving prank with Pansy Lane
segments.summary: Loyacano says he was called Hook; Crawford mentions Daniel Mello's story of him and Pansy Lane, and Loyacano describes getting their heads shaved with a razor for fun.

segments.title: Ragtime to Dixieland, fifty years playing, and his birth date
segments.summary: His wife explains the shift from ragtime to Dixieland; Loyacano says he played 50 years, stopped in January 1959 and was born October 14, 1893.

segments.title: Teaching himself trombone on the pianola
segments.summary: He took no lessons, learning trombone by pumping the pianola with his feet and playing with hands and mouth.

segments.title: His brothers Arnold, Jack and Bud and their instruments
segments.summary: He names three musical brothers and what each played, including Jack the left-handed trombonist.

segments.title: Slide trombone and the ragtime tunes of the early days
segments.summary: He started on slide trombone, heard old-time jazz called ragtime, and cannot recall tune names after fifty years.

segments.title: First bands: Jack Lane's Reliance, Pansy Lane, and Dan Hughes on Canal Street
segments.summary: He lists his first bands and describes advertising Lou Rose's show by walking Canal Street, and Dan Hughes the one-eyed trumpeter.

segments.title: Who played in Jack Lane's and Pansy Lane's bands
segments.summary: He cannot recall Jack Lane's men, being 16, but names Foots Mello, Harry Shields and Pansy in Pansy Lane's band.

segments.title: Joe Ellibush's band and lawn party jobs on bass horn
segments.summary: With Joe Ellibush, a poor trombonist who led the band, he played bass horn at lawn parties without piano.

segments.title: Valve trombone, vamp style and trombone range in the early days
segments.summary: He discusses Bill Gallaty's valve trombone, his own vamp bass-part style, and the low range used, noting he never read music then.

segments.title: The failed lesson with the Orpheum trombonist Wickfold
segments.summary: A trombonist teacher refused his money because Loyacano's ear kept him a split second behind and he played everything by ear.

segments.chapter: Photographs, reading music and Wingy Manone
segments.title: Photographs: Sharkey at the Silver Slipper and the Biloxi Elks Club band
segments.summary: Looking at pictures, he identifies the players in a Mardi Gras band with Sharkey and a Biloxi Elks Club band with Johnny Bertucci.

segments.chapter: Photographs, reading music and Wingy Manone
segments.title: Learning to read music with Max Fink at the Lill Club
segments.summary: He learned to read by following parts as sousaphone player for Max Fink and ends with a Biloxi newspaper date for the photograph.

segments.chapter: Photographs, reading music and Wingy Manone
segments.title: Peck Kelly rumor and working with Wingy Manone in San Antonio
segments.summary: He knew Peck Kelly but never worked with him, and says he played in Texas with Wingy Manone.

segments.chapter: Photographs, reading music and Wingy Manone
segments.title: Wingy Manone's bands in San Antonio and at the Buena Vista Hotel
segments.summary: He recalls personnel of Wingy's San Antonio band and of the Buena Vista and White House hotel band.

segments.chapter: Club Forest and the Halfway House
segments.title: Duke Yandis in Cincinnati, Max Fink in Memphis, 22 months at Club Forest
segments.summary: He recounts the Gibson Hotel job, Memphis with Max Fink and 22 solid months at Club Forest under Charlie Fish, Jules Bauduc and Duke Yandis.

segments.chapter: Club Forest and the Halfway House
segments.title: Club Forest trumpeters and Emmett Hardy's brilliance
segments.summary: He recalls Tony Almerico, Red Bowman, and especially Emmett Hardy and his band, including Louis Armstrong's praise on the excursion boat.

segments.chapter: Club Forest and the Halfway House
segments.title: Records with Brunis and the Halfway House band photograph
segments.summary: They look at records he made with Brunis and identify the two trombone tunes, Barataria and Pussycat Rag.

segments.chapter: Club Forest and the Halfway House
segments.title: Steady job at the Halfway House and its personnel
segments.summary: He identifies the Halfway House band members, Rappolo's condition, and says he worked there three or four years during Prohibition.

segments.chapter: Working life: spot jobs, day jobs, nightclubs
segments.title: Spot work, fraternity dances and Sunday picnics
segments.summary: He preferred spot jobs, worked nightly with Brownlee and Hardy on fraternity dances, and played Sunday picnics for good money.

segments.chapter: Working life: spot jobs, day jobs, nightclubs
segments.title: Jimmy Wakely's offer to go to California
segments.summary: He turned down a three thousand dollar a year offer from hillbilly entertainer Jimmy Wakely because of his family.

segments.chapter: Working life: spot jobs, day jobs, nightclubs
segments.title: Day jobs and musicians at the McGinnis cotton mill
segments.summary: Most musicians had day jobs; he worked at the cotton mill alongside other musicians.

segments.chapter: Working life: spot jobs, day jobs, nightclubs
segments.title: Night club work at Pete Herman's and Dixie's ball music
segments.summary: He played bass at Pete Herman's for thirty-five a week and with Dixie on St. Charles Street, and talks about Duranti.

segments.chapter: Working life: spot jobs, day jobs, nightclubs
segments.title: How picnic jobs worked and what tunes they played
segments.summary: At picnics he played from nine to six with breaks, without pianos, doing polkas, foxtrots, one steps and waltzes.

segments.chapter: Early bands and New Orleans musicians
segments.title: The Triangle Band and the Majana brothers
segments.summary: He played trombone in the Majana brothers' spot-job Triangle Band, quit after a dispute, and talk turns to Sato and Steve Woodrow's wife.

segments.chapter: Early bands and New Orleans musicians
segments.title: Dan Hughes's band: Ballet Rite and Clem Camp
segments.summary: They recall the drummer and clarinetist of Dan Hughes's band, with Loyacano on trombone and his brother Bud on bass horn.

segments.chapter: Early bands and New Orleans musicians
segments.title: Brother Bud in a nursing home and Joe's stroke
segments.summary: Crawford wants to interview Bud, who has a good memory; his wife explains Joe's stroke two years earlier damaged his memory.

segments.chapter: Early bands and New Orleans musicians
segments.title: Henry Fillmore pieces, brass bands, and Jack Teagarden as favorite
segments.summary: He never played Fillmore pieces or brass bands, and names Jack Teagarden as his favorite trombonist, soon to play the Dream Room.

segments.chapter: Early bands and New Orleans musicians
segments.title: Early New Orleans trombonists: Brunis, Gallaty, Ellibush, Perkins
segments.summary: He assesses the trombone players he knew, who played Dixieland and who read.

segments.chapter: Early bands and New Orleans musicians
segments.title: Outstanding trumpeters and drummers
segments.summary: Emmett Hardy was top trumpeter; he also names other trumpeters and good Dixieland drummers like Buck Rogers and Monk Hazel.

segments.chapter: Early bands and New Orleans musicians
segments.title: Eddie Edwards and Jackson School
segments.summary: They discuss Eddie Edwards, who played violin for marching at Jackson School.

segments.chapter: Early bands and New Orleans musicians
segments.title: No church music; lawn parties and their drinks and admission
segments.summary: He never played in church; lawn parties were in backyards with drinks and a small entry charge.

segments.chapter: Early bands and New Orleans musicians
segments.title: Born on Magazine Street and musicians in the neighborhood
segments.summary: He was born at 1364 Magazine Street; the Majanas and Woodrow lived near him.

segments.title: Working with Leon and Louis Prima and at the Pumpkin
segments.summary: He worked with Leon Prima at the Avalon Club and with Louis, and at the Pumpkin with Leo Hade on drums.

segments.title: Chicago with brother Deacon, Bill Brady and Yellow Nunez
segments.summary: He played at 58th and State in Chicago in Bill Brady's band with his drummer brother, and with Yellow Nunez.

segments.title: First recording sessions: Brunis, Shockey, Almerico
segments.summary: His first recording was with Abby Brunis; later he recorded with Shockey and Almerico.

segments.title: String bass, sousaphone and upright bass horns early on
segments.summary: He explains that early bands used string bass, with a few upright bass horns rather than sousaphones.

segments.title: Mario Fanats, the best bass player
segments.summary: He praises Fanats, a big man whose upright horn sounded like a bass fiddle, and talks about his sons.

segments.title: Wiffle Rogers and Tala's beer garden
segments.summary: They discuss the Rogers brothers and Tala's beer garden in Ottoman Park, with its tree through the building and Mike Trepani's band.

segments.title: Jules Bauduc's ten-piece reading band at Club Forest
segments.summary: The Bauduc band was mostly reading with special arrangements and little jazz.

segments.title: His father, bass as a boy, and serenading Italian family music
segments.summary: He played bass as a boy standing on a box; his father played in an Italian waltz group that serenaded at night, and the Brunettes had a family band.

segments.title: Neighborhood trumpeters: Shellans, Zimmerman, Heinz brothers
segments.summary: They recall neighbors and musicians such as Gus Zimmerman and the Heinz brothers, with some confusion.

segments.title: Clarinet, saxophone, piano and banjo players he knew
segments.summary: He names Rappolo, Cadela, Scaglione, Eddie Powers, Mickey Marcour and Billy Eastwood.

segments.title: Photographs from Tom Brown's collection and the Spanish Fort jazzers
segments.summary: They look at old pictures including the Jazzola Novelty Orchestra at Spanish Fort and discuss the collector brother who found them.

segments.title: Steve Brown and slap bass technique
segments.summary: He praises Steve Brown and explains slapping bass strings against the fingerboard, like a wood block.

segments.title: Seventeen years with Tony Almerico and Abby Brunis's death
segments.summary: His wife says he spotted with everyone; he was with Tony Almerico 17 years and they recall Abby Brunis dying in Chicago.

segments.title: Recording at the Halfway House sessions and the old studio
segments.summary: They discuss where the Halfway House recording was made and that it used electric microphones, 33 years earlier.

segments.title: Records for Tony, Joe Moretz and the Rosemary Clooney release problem
segments.summary: He made many records with Tony and for Joe Moretz, one unreleased because Rosemary Clooney sang on it.

segments.title: The many Loyacanos, Mike Lalla and Bourbon Street players
segments.summary: His wife explains unrelated Loyacano musicians; talk moves to Mike Lalla, Bourbon Street groups and the Confederate colonels.

segments.title: End of the tape
segments.summary: A no-cash job comment, and Crawford ends the tape.
